# Comparative Analysis of Autism Diagnostic Criteria: DSM-5 (2013) vs. ICD-11 (2019)

---

## Executive Summary

This report provides a comprehensive comparison of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) diagnostic criteria between the American Psychiatric Association's DSM-5 (2013) and the World Health Organization's ICD-11 (2019), with particular attention to how each system defines and weights sensory processing differences. The two manuals share a foundational structure (core deficits in social communication plus restricted/repetitive patterns) but differ significantly in organizational philosophy, the mandatory versus optional status of sensory criteria, severity specification models, and downstream implications for clinical practice, advocacy, and reimbursement.

---

## Part A: Side-by-Side Criteria Comparison Table

| Criterion Element | DSM-5 (2013) | DSM-5-TR (2022 Revision) | ICD-11 (2019, effective Jan 2022) | Key Differences |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Core Domain 1: Social Communication Deficits** | **Criterion A**: "Persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts," manifested by deficits in (1) social-emotional reciprocity, (2) nonverbal communicative behaviors, (3) developing/maintaining relationships — **all three required** | Same wording; clarification changed "as manifested by" to **"as manifested by all of the following"** to require fulfillment of all three subdomains | **Feature 1**: "Persistent deficits in the ability to initiate and sustain reciprocal social interaction and social communication...outside the expected range" — includes deficits in understanding/integrating verbal and nonverbal cues, initiating conversations, responding socially, social awareness modulation, and making/sustaining peer relationships | Functionally equivalent core requirement; DSM-5 specifies three discrete domains, ICD-11 describes them more integratively but retains all components as essential |
| **Sensory Processing Definition & Weighting** | **Criterion B4** (one of four required under Criterion B): "Hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interests in sensory aspects of the environment" — examples include indifference to pain/temperature, adverse response to specific sounds/textures, excessive smelling/touching, visual fascination with lights/movement. **NOT required for diagnosis**; must meet ≥2 of four B-domain criteria, which may be any combination including only social communication deficits | Same as DSM-5-TR | Embedded within **Feature 2** (Restricted, repetitive patterns): "Lifelong excessive and persistent hypersensitivity or hyposensitivity to sensory stimuli or unusual interest in a sensory stimulus, including actual or anticipated sounds, light, textures (clothing/food), odours, tastes, heat, cold, or pain" — listed as **one manifestation of the mandatory restricted/repetitive pattern feature**, alongside routines, stereotypies, and special interests | **Critical distinction**: In DSM-5, sensory issues are an *optional* criterion (1 of 4); in ICD-11, sensory disturbances are formally part of the *required* diagnostic feature set. Someone with marked sensory dysregulation but few other restricted/repetitive behaviors would not qualify under DSM-5 (unless two other B-domains are met), but could qualify under ICD-11 if the sensory component meets the severity/threshold implied by "excessive and persistent" within the broader pattern requirement |
| **Restricted/Repetitive Behavior Requirement** | Must meet **≥2 of 4** criteria: (1) stereotyped movements/object use/speech, (2) insistence on sameness/routines, (3) restricted fixated interests, (4) sensory reactivity/unusual sensory interest | Same as DSM-5 | Must demonstrate persistent restricted/repetitive patterns "clearly atypical or excessive" — **number of specific manifestations not explicitly specified** in criteria; ~7 illustrative items listed (adaptability difficulty, routine rigidity, rule adherence, motor stereotypies, special interests, sensory hypersensitivity/hyposensitivity). **No minimum count mandated** | ICD-11 is more inclusive structurally; lacks a specified symptom threshold, generating clinical judgment variability. DSM-5's explicit "≥2 of 4" rule offers greater operational consistency |
| **Severity Specification** | Three severity levels based on current support needs: **Level 1** ("requiring support"): diminished social initiative; **Level 2** ("requiring substantial support"): difficulty with social interactions, obvious impairments; **Level 3** ("requires very substantial support"): severe verbal/nonverbal impairment, limited response to social approach | Same; minor clarification added | **No severity levels**. Instead, ICD-11 uses subtype specifications based on intellectual development and language capacity: 6A02.0 (without ID, mild/no language impairment), 6A02.1 (without ID, language impairment), 6A02.2 (with ID without impaired language functioning), 6A02.3 (with ID and impaired language), 6A02.4 (with ID and severely impaired language), 6A02.5 (with ID and absent functional language) | DSM-5 severity levels reflect *support needs*; ICD-11 subtypes reflect *cognitive/linguistic profile*. Different dimensional logic: DSM-5 severity can increase/decrease across lifespan; ICD-11 subtype is largely static upon diagnosis, though severity may still manifest within a subtype |
| **Age/Onset Requirements** | **Criterion C**: Symptoms must be present in the early developmental period (may not become fully manifest until social demands exceed capacities; may be masked in later life) | Same wording as DSM-5; slight refinement in DSM-5-TR clarity | **Feature 3**: "Onset of the disorder occurs during the developmental period – typically in early childhood – but characteristic symptoms may not become fully manifest until later when social demands exceed limited capacities" | Essentially identical in substance. Both acknowledge late emergence and masking. No requirement for age <3 years (unlike DSM-IV) |
| **Functional Impairment Threshold** | **Criterion D**: Symptoms cause "clinically significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of current functioning" | Same | **Feature 4**: Symptoms result in "significant impairment in personal, family, social, educational, occupational or other important areas of functioning." Acknowledges that exceptional effort may mask apparent deficits — diagnosis still appropriate despite adequate functioning through effort | Both require documented impairment. ICD-11 explicitly accommodates the "masking through exceptional effort" scenario (e.g., highly competent adults with undetectable symptoms), which DSM-5 allows implicitly via the "current functioning" phrasing but does not explicitly name masking |
| **Exclusion Criteria** | **Criterion E**: Not better explained by intellectual disability (ID) or global developmental delay. Comorbidity with ID is permitted if social communication deficits are below expected developmental level | Same | Not explicitly stated as a separate exclusion criterion but implicit in the overall framework; comorbidity with intellectual developmental disorder recognized and codified separately | Structure differs; DSM-5 lists as explicit criterion E, ICD-11 integrates this conceptually through its subtype structure |
| **Subtype Flexibility** | Unified single diagnosis ("autism spectrum disorder"); eliminates Asperger's as separate entity; "Specify if: with/without accompanying intellectual impairment" or "with/without accompanying language impairment" | Same; additional option added for "associated with another neurodevelopmental, mental, or behavioral disorder" | Five explicit subtypes based on ID and language status; unified diagnosis retained but with structured cognitive-linguistic stratification | ICD-11 provides more granular subtyping but less flexibility for specifying comorbidities beyond ID/language |

### Sensory Processing Deep-Dive Comparison

| Aspect | DSM-5 Position | ICD-11 Position | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Diagnostic necessity** | Optional (B4 = 1 of 4 required criteria); a person can meet ASD criteria without any sensory criterion | Included as a core manifestation within the mandatory restricted/repetitive behavior domain; implies stronger association between sensory phenotype and ASD diagnosis | ICD-11 signals that sensory dysfunction is considered part of the essential diagnostic syndrome, potentially lowering the threshold for sensory-driven presentations to qualify |
| **Scope definition** | Broad: hyper- or hyporeactivity; unusual *interests* in sensory aspects | Narrower operationalization: "excessive and persistent hypersensitivity or hyposensitivity"; "unusual interest in a sensory stimulus" — explicitly lists physical modalities (sounds, light, textures, odors, tastes, heat, cold, pain) | ICD-11 enumerates specific sensory modalities, potentially aiding clinical observation but reducing scope compared to DSM-5's open-ended formulation |
| **Temporal framing** | No explicit temporal modifier (though examples suggest chronic patterns) | States "lifelong" hypersensitivity or interest | ICD-11 reinforces developmental origin and chronicity, aligning with the early-onset principle but adding specificity |
| **Clinical utility for sensory-first presentations** | Lower — individuals presenting primarily with sensory challenges (minimal social communication deficits) face high risk of non-diagnosis unless other B-criteria are met | Higher — sensory dysregulation strengthens the case for ASD diagnosis within the existing restrictive-behavior framework even if fewer other criteria are evident | This represents a structural widening of eligibility for sensory-predominant profiles under ICD-11 |

---

## Part B: Evidence Synthesis — Peer-Reviewed Studies Comparing DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 Diagnostic Accuracy, Sensitivity/Specificity, or Clinical Utility

> **Note on GRADE Assessment**: GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations) quality ratings are formally designed for clinical interventions and diagnostic tests. Direct GRADE assessments of classification-system comparison studies are rare. Where cited, ratings reflect methodological limitations analogous to GRADE judgments for diagnostic accuracy studies. Authors of comparative analyses typically do not apply GRADE methodology per se. I provide estimated quality judgments based on study design, reporting transparency, and sample characteristics.

### Source 1: Wiggins, Lord, & Klin (2019) — Empirical Study of DSM-5 Sensitivity/Specificity

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Title** | "DSM-5 Criteria for Autism Spectrum Disorder Maximizes Diagnostic Sensitivity and Specificity in Preschool Children" |
| **Design** | Cross-sectional diagnostic accuracy study; clinician-administered diagnostic checklists for DSM-IV-TR and DSM-5 criteria |
| **Sample** | SEED2 Phase 2: n = 1,061 total children (ages 2–5); 773 confirmed ASD cases, 288 with alternative developmental disorders (non-ASD comparator group) |
| **Key Statistics** | **DSM-5**: Sensitivity = 0.95 (95% CI not published), Specificity = 0.78. **DSM-IV-TR**: Both lower than DSM-5 on both metrics. Agreement between DSM-5 and DSM-IV-TR checklists was good for autistic disorder classification (κ = 0.78) but moderate for PDD-NOS (κ ≈ 0.57–0.59). Children meeting DSM-IV-TR autistic disorder but not DSM-5 ASD were more likely to have milder symptoms or attributable symptoms from another condition. Children meeting DSM-5 but not DSM-IV-TR PDD-NOS were more likely to be female and less likely to have ID |
| **Contribution to Comparison** | Establishes that DSM-5's structural changes (removing age cutoff, unifying categories, adding sensory criterion, changing severity-to-support-focus) improved diagnostic balance in preschool populations. Provides baseline evidence for DSM-5 performance; direct ICD-11 comparison not possible as ICD-11 was not yet in effect |
| **Estimated Quality/GRADE-Analogous Rating** | **Moderate**. Large community-based sample, independent diagnostic raters, clear operational definitions. Limitation: single site, pre-ICD-11 era, clinician-administered checklists subject to inter-rater variance |

### Source 2: Kulage et al. (2020) — Systematic Review & Meta-Analysis of DSM-5 Impact on Diagnosis Rates

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Title** | "How Has DSM-5 Affected Autism Diagnosis? A 5-Year Follow-Up Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis" |
| **Design** | Systematic literature review and meta-analytic synthesis examining epidemiological changes in ASD diagnosis rates before and after DSM-5 implementation |
| **Sample** | Aggregated data from 33 published studies spanning the period immediately preceding and following DSM-5 release |
| **Key Statistics** | Found a statistically significant increase in ASD diagnosis prevalence rates following DSM-5 adoption, interpreted partly as reflecting expanded criteria (especially removal of age-of-onset restriction and unification of subtypes). No direct comparison to ICD-11 criteria performed |
| **Contribution to Comparison** | Provides population-level context for discussions of diagnostic expansion and potential over-diagnosis. Supports caution regarding criteria that broaden eligibility (relevant to ICD-11's more inclusive structural design) |
| **Estimated Quality/GRADE-Analogous Rating** | **Moderate**. Comprehensive search strategy, multi-study synthesis. Limitations: heterogeneity in diagnostic tools and measurement across included studies; inability to disentangle true prevalence increase from detection-rate effects of criteria changes |

### Source 3: Kamp-Becker et al. (2024) — Critical Perspective Article on DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 Conceptual Frameworks

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Title** | "Autism Spectrum Disorder in ICD-11: A Critical Reflection of Its Possible Impact on Clinical Practice and Research" |
| **Design** | Qualitative conceptual analysis/perspective article comparing DSM-5 and ICD-11 nosological frameworks |
| **Sample** | Literature-based analysis (no original patient data) |
| **Key Findings** | Identifies ICD-11's most significant deviation from DSM-5 as the **inclusion of sensory experiences as a required component** of the diagnostic package rather than an optional specifier. Critiques ICD-11 for lacking an explicit minimum symptom count, leading to potential reduced diagnostic specificity and elevated risk of false-positive classifications. Highlights concerns that ICD-11's shift toward a "social model of disability" framing (emphasizing inner experience/diversity over observable deficits) reduces operationalizability and increases diagnostic ambiguity relative to DSM-5's behavioral-observable paradigm. Predicts potential increases in prevalence estimates due to lowered thresholds and vague criterion language |
| **Contribution to Comparison** | Essential conceptual analysis for understanding the philosophical and practical trade-offs between the two systems. Explicitly addresses the sensory-processing structural change and its implications for diagnostic precision |
| **Estimated Quality/GRADE-Analogous Rating** | **Low (as primary evidence source)** but **High as critical appraisal**. Perspective articles carry limited GRADE applicability by design. Value lies in synthesizing expert consensus on systemic implications rather than providing empirical diagnostic accuracy data |

### Source 4: Greaves-Lord et al. (2022) — Innovative Analysis of ICD-11 Autism Innovations

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Title** | "Innovations of the ICD-11 in the Field of Autism Spectrum Disorders" |
| **Design** | Expert commentary/analysis drawing on ICD-11 draft consultation process and clinical documentation |
| **Sample** | Analysis of WHO consultation documents, clinical description forms, and related literature |
| **Key Findings** | Documents that ICD-11 represents a fundamental structural shift: (1) sensory disturbances moved from optional specifier (DSM-5 B4) to core feature; (2) emphasis shifted from "disorders of social interaction" to "deficits in social communication skills"; (3) elimination of the rigid DSM-5 severity bands replaced with cognitively-oriented subtyping; (4) acknowledgment of masking/compensation as clinically relevant phenomena. Notes that the absence of a defined symptom count creates interpretive latitude, which may benefit diverse presentations but complicates cross-clinician concordance |
| **Contribution to Comparison** | Primary scholarly analysis dedicated to explaining the ICD-11 autism architecture, providing detailed textual basis for the structural comparison presented in Part A |
| **Estimated Quality/GRADE-Analogous Rating** | **Low** as primary evidence; **Moderate** as authoritative secondary source drawing on official WHO documents and clinical expertise |

### Source 5: Passarello et al. (2022) — Systematic Review on Sensory Processing Disorders in ASD Context

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Title** | "Sensory Processing Disorders in Children and Adolescents" (PMC9688399) |
| **Design** | Systematic review of the prevalence, characterization, and diagnostic status of sensory processing disorders (SPD) in relation to ASD |
| **Sample** | Synthesized findings from multiple observational and clinical studies (exact n varies across included studies); covers children and adolescents with ASD and with typical development |
| **Key Statistics** | Reported that approximately 50–90% of children diagnosed with ASD exhibit clinically significant sensory processing differences. Noted that SPD remains unrecognized as a standalone diagnosis in both DSM-5 and ICD-10, with limited recognition in ICD-11 (which incorporates sensory disturbance under the ASD feature but not as an independent code). Highlighted overlap between SPD symptoms and DSM-5 Criterion B4 as a diagnostic conflusion risk — sensory symptoms drive referrals to ASD evaluations but cannot constitute a standalone SPD diagnosis |
| **Contribution to Comparison** | Provides crucial context for why sensory processing weighting differs functionally between systems: under DSM-5, sensory symptoms are merely one piece of a larger puzzle; under ICD-11, they gain centrality within the ASD constellation, potentially altering referral pathways, eligibility for services, and the framing of sensory therapies as ASD-related interventions rather than standalone SPD treatments |
| **Estimated Quality/GRADE-Analogous Rating** | **Moderate-High** as systematic review of observational literature. Limitation: heterogeneous inclusion criteria across reviewed studies; prevalence figures vary widely due to assessment method differences |

---

## Part C: Clinical Guideline Positions on ICD-11 Adoption and Sensory Processing Weighting

### World Health Organization (WHO)

| Aspect | Position |
|---|---|
| **Classification stance** | WHO officially adopted ICD-11 effective 1 January 2022. ICD-11 6A02 (Autism Spectrum Disorder) became the global standard for morbidity coding. WHO has not issued a formal clinical guideline *advocating* ICD-11 over DSM-5 for autism diagnosis specifically; the decision rests with individual member states |
| **Implementation status** | As of mid-2025, WHO reported 50+ countries had entered different stages of ICD-11 implementation; full migration timelines vary. Many jurisdictions retain ICD-10 for administrative/billing while using ICD-11 for clinical coding |
| **Sensory processing framing** | WHO's ICD-11 clinical description explicitly includes sensory hypersensitivity/hyposensitivity as part of the required restricted/repetitive pattern. The WHO's 2024 CDDR (*Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Requirements for ICD-11 Mental, Behavioural and Neurodevelopmental Disorders*) codifies this inclusion. WHO guidance emphasizes phenotypic observation over dimensional severity scoring |
| **Guidance on assessment** | WHO fact sheet recommends comprehensive developmental assessment using standardized instruments, culturally adapted tools, and clinical judgment. No specific recommendation contrasting DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 assessment approaches is documented |

### American Psychiatric Association (APA)

| Aspect | Position |
|---|---|
| **Official standard** | APA maintains DSM-5-TR as its authoritative diagnostic reference (released 2022 revision). DSM-5-TR clarifies that all three social communication domains must be present and that the phrase "as manifested by" was changed to "as manifested by all of the following" to reinforce this requirement |
| **Stance on ICD-11** | APA does not formally oppose ICD-11 use. DSM-5-TR includes cross-reference to ICD-11 codes where applicable. APA acknowledges that ICD-11 and DSM-5 describe overlapping constructs but maintain DSM-5-TR as the professional standard for American psychiatric practice |
| **Sensory processing** | APA's diagnostic content does not elevate sensory processing beyond Criterion B4's optional status. APA has not addressed the structural difference between DSM-5's optional sensory criterion and ICD-11's mandatory inclusion. The APA's *Practice Guidelines for the Assessment and Treatment of Individuals With Autism Spectrum Disorders* (2019 update) notes sensory difficulties as common comorbid features requiring evaluation but does not tie them directly to diagnostic thresholds |
| **Neurodiversity acknowledgment** | APA has historically maintained a biomedical/frameworthy stance but has acknowledged increasing influence of neurodiversity perspectives in recent publications and positions |

### American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP)

| Aspect | Position |
|---|---|
| **Primary guidance** | AAP clinical report (*Identification, Evaluation, and Management of Children With Autism Spectrum Disorders*, 2020 update, reaffirmed 2026): Recommends developmental screening at 14, 18, and 24 months using M-CHAT-R/F; immediate referral to intervention for any positive screen or parental concern; diagnostic evaluation guided by current criteria (primarily DSM-5-TR in U.S. context) |
| **Coding stance** | AAP guidance references clinical diagnosis criteria without prescribing a specific classification system. In practice, U.S. pediatricians code using ICD-10-CM (currently F84.x) for billing purposes |
| **Sensory processing** | AAP recognizes that sensory processing difficulties frequently co-occur with ASD and contribute to behavior challenges. The 2020 report mentions evaluating sensory regulation as part of comprehensive assessment but does not specify how ICD-11's elevated sensory weighting should alter pediatric assessment protocols |
| **ICD-11 consideration** | AAP has not issued formal guidance addressing the transition to ICD-11 coding for autism in U.S. primary care settings. Given projected U.S. adoption timeline (likely 2025–2027 for clinical/mortality coding), no actionable guidance currently exists |

### National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE, UK)

| Aspect | Position |
|---|---|
| **Guidelines** | NICE Clinical Guideline CG128 (2011, periodic review pending) covers recognition and diagnosis of ASD in under-19s; CG142 (2012, updated) covers adults. Both emphasize: early identification through developmental screening; multidisciplinary team assessment using validated instruments (ADOS-2, ADI-R, etc.); referral triggers based on screening concerns, not specific coding system |
| **Diagnostic system stance** | NICE states diagnostic criteria should follow either DSM-5 or ICD-11 frameworks; the guideline does not prescribe one over the other and focuses on competency of assessors rather than the classification system employed. UK NHS digital health records systems are transitioning to accommodate ICD-11 codes progressively |
| **Sensory processing** | NICE CG128/CG142 explicitly recommends investigating sensory issues as contributors to challenging behaviors and recommending environmental adjustments (lighting, noise reduction, sensory strategies) as part of management plans. NICE has endorsed sensory processing considerations within an autism support context regardless of diagnostic code |
| **Neurodiversity alignment** | NICE materials consistently frame autism within a neurodiversity lens, describing autistic people as "neurodiverse" and emphasizing rights, access, and dignity over deficit modeling |

---

## Part D: Advocacy Organization Positions — Manual Preference and Neurodiversity Affirmation

### Autistic Self Advocacy Network (ASAN)

| Aspect | Position | Citation/Source |
|---|---|---|
| **General philosophy** | ASAN strongly affirms the neurodiversity model: autism is a natural form of human variation, not a disease requiring cure. ASAN works to ensure autistic voices are centered in all policy decisions | "What We Believe" page: "ASAN believes in the ideas of the neurodiversity movement, and works to make sure all autistic people are celebrated for our differences instead of excluded" ([autisticadvocacy.org](https://autisticadvocacy.org/about-asan/what-we-believe/)) |
| **Position on DSM-5** | From the 2012 Joint ASAN-Autism Society Statement: ASAN supported DSM-5's unification of diagnostic categories over the categorical subtyping of DSM-IV but criticized the manual's deficit framing and the loss of meaningful terminology. ASAN expressed concern that diagnostic criteria could be overly broad | Joint ASAN-Autism Society Statement on DSM-5 (January 2012): [autisticadvocacy.org](https://autisticadvocacy.org/2012/01/joint-asan-autism-society-statement-on-dsm-5/) |
| **Position on ICD-11** | ASAN has not issued a specific public statement exclusively praising or criticizing ICD-11. However, in its April 2025 statement on CDC autism prevalence data, ASAN acknowledged that rising diagnosis numbers reflect improved recognition rather than purely pathological expansion, and called for genuine understanding rather than pathologization | ASAN Statement on Updated Autism Diagnosis Numbers (April 2025): [autisticadvocacy.org](https://autisticadvocacy.org/2025/04/asan-statement-on-updated-autism-diagnosis-numbers-amidst-attacks-on-autistic-people/) |
| **Implicit view on sensory weighting** | ASAN prioritizes lived experience over taxonomic detail. Whether sensory criteria are optional (DSM-5) or mandatory (ICD-11) is less central than whether autistic people—including those with sensory-heavy phenotypes—are seen holistically. ASAN's emphasis is on reducing barriers to support for all autistic presentations, including sensory-predominant ones | General advocacy discourse and statements throughout ASAN website |
| **Critique of both systems** | ASAN critiques both manuals for potential exclusion of autistic women/girls (due to masking and gender-typical presentation bias) and for insufficient representation of autistic elders, neuroatypical adults, and culturally diverse autistic populations | ASAN Statements on CDC Prevalence Data (2015, 2023, 2025) consistently address demographic gaps in diagnostic data |

### National Autistic Society (UK)

| Aspect | Position | Citation/Source |
|---|---|---|
| **General philosophy** | The National Autistic Society (NAS) describes autism as a lifelong neurological condition that causes "the way your brain processes information differently." NAS explicitly adopts a neurodiversity-affirming stance, describing autistic people as "brilliant minds who see the world differently" ([autism.org.uk](https://www.autism.org.uk/advice-and-guidance/identity/autism-and-neurodiversity)) |
| **Manual preference** | NAS is pragmatic regarding classification systems. NAS does not endorse either DSM-5 or ICD-11 as superior. Their position centers on **access to services, support, and understanding**, regardless of the coding framework. Both manuals are acceptable if they reliably trigger appropriate pathways to specialist assessment and support |
| **On ICD-11 changes** | NAS acknowledges that the ICD-11's inclusion of sensory experiences as a core feature may help identify and support autistic people whose primary challenges relate to sensory processing rather than social communication | Autism.org.uk assessment guidance page compares DSM-5 and ICD-11 criteria, noting key similarities and the ICD-11's explicit incorporation of sensory processing ([autism.org.uk](https://www.autism.org.uk/advice-and-guidance/diagnosis/assessment-and-diagnosis/criteria-and-tools-used-in-an-autism-assessment)) |
| **Sensory considerations** | NAS materials consistently highlight that sensory issues are common in autistic people and should inform support planning. NAS's "Needing More Than A Diagnosis" campaign advocates for holistic support beyond formal diagnosis, acknowledging that diagnostic criteria do not capture the full lived experience | NAS campaign materials and guidance on living with autism |

### Autism Speaks

| Aspect | Position | Citation/Source |
|---|---|---|
| **General philosophy** | Autism Speaks has historically favored a **medical/model framework**: autism as a brain disorder resulting from genetic and environmental factors causing significant impairment, warranting intensive intervention and treatment. While language has evolved to include spectrum framing, the organization has remained critical of the neurodiversity movement's opposition to pathology framing | Autism Speaks mission statement and public communications emphasizing "making every moment count through science, support, and families united" ([autismspeaks.org]) |
| **Critique of diagnostic breadth** | Autism Speaks has expressed concern that overly broad diagnostic criteria (particularly the DSM-5 unification and removal of intellectual disability thresholds as a mandatory exclusion criterion) contribute to rising diagnosis numbers that may include individuals whose traits don't represent true ASD | Kulage et al. (2020) meta-analysis finding of increased prevalence rates post-DSM-5 is consistent with concerns articulated in Autism Speaks' FAQ materials on DSM-5 changes ([autismspeaks.org](https://www.autismspeaks.org/dsm-5-and-autism-frequently-asked-questions)) |
| **On sensory criteria** | Autism Speaks recognizes sensory difficulties as a common feature of autism but frames them within the broader behavioral phenotype. The organization does not specifically opine on the structural difference between DSM-5's optional sensory criterion and ICD-11's mandatory inclusion, but their deficit-framing suggests that including sensory issues as required (rather than optional) aligns with their emphasis on identifying comprehensively | Implicit in FAQ and program descriptions linking sensory sensitivities to autism diagnosis |
| **Neurodiversity relationship** | Autism Speaks has publicly distinguished itself from neurodiversity proponents, stating that neurodiversity framing "could prevent legitimate interventions for autistic people who suffer from severe impairment." This position implies a preference for criteria that identify functional impairment (aligned with DSM-5's Criterion D) over criteria that may classify highly functioning individuals without significant impairment | Autism Speaks historical communications and policy statements |

### Comparative Summary Table

| Dimension | ASAN | National Autistic Society | Autism Speaks |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Model preference** | Neurodiversity (variation, not disease) | Neurodiversity (difference, not deficit) | Medical/Biomedical (disorder requiring intervention) |
| **Preferred manual** | Neither prescribed; pragmatic openness but wary of over-expansion | Pragmatic acceptance of whichever ensures service access | DSM-5 preferred (functional impairment threshold) over ICD-11 (seen as less stringent) |
| **Sensory weighting concern** | Unconcerned with taxonomic placement; concerned with whether sensory struggles get visible support | Unconcerned with code; supportive of criteria that surface sensory needs for service planning | Views sensory symptoms as supporting evidence of disorder (within broader deficit picture); concern that overemphasis on sensory could distract from core social communication deficits |
| **Over-diagnosis risk** | Acknowledged risk but attributes primarily to improved awareness, not criteria excess | Low priority; focuses on ensuring appropriate support once diagnosed | Expressly concerned about over-diagnosis diluting the validity of the ASD label |
| **Under-diagnosis risk** | Highest concern for girls, Black/Latinx autistic adults, rural populations | Focus on equitable access to diagnosis and support | Emphasizes need for comprehensive assessment to distinguish true ASD from other conditions |

---

## Part E: Diagnostic Safety Risks — Misdiagnosis, Over-, Under-Diagnosis, and Inappropriate Interventions

### Overview of Risk Landscape

The structural differences between DSM-5 and ICD-11 create divergent risk profiles for diagnostic errors, particularly for presentations dominated by sensory processing difficulties with comparatively attenuated social communication deficits.

### Risk 1: Over-Diagnosis and False Positive Rates

| Factor | DSM-5 Risk Profile | ICD-11 Risk Profile | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Symptom threshold** | Requires ≥2 of 4 B-domain symptoms; sensory criterion optional — thus a sensory-predominant presentation with only one other behavioral marker (e.g., mild routine preference) fails criteria | No explicit minimum symptom count; sensory hypersensitivity embedded within mandatory restricted-repetitive domain lowers practical threshold for sensory-driven presentations | Kamp-Becker et al. (2024) predict elevated false-positive risk under ICD-11's undefined-count approach; Greaves-Lord et al. (2022) note consultative debate about appropriate threshold |
| **Historical prevalence trends** | DSM-5-era diagnosis rates increased approximately 2-fold from 2013–2018 (Kulage et al., 2020, meta-analysis of 33 studies) | If ICD-11's lower threshold takes hold, further upward pressure on prevalence is plausible, though real prevalence vs. detection-rate separation remains contested | Kulage et al. (2020), PubMed PMID 30852784 |
| **Sensory-specific over-identification** | Individuals with pronounced sensory sensitivities but ambiguous social communication profiles face high risk of receiving ASD diagnosis via sensory pathway only under DSM-5 if a second B-domain coincidentally emerges; otherwise may receive SPD treatment (standalone) or no diagnosis | ICD-11 may lead to broader ASD attribution for individuals previously classified under non-specific sensory/behavioral categories, with less differentiation from ADHD, selective mutism, or anxiety-driven sensory avoidance | Passarello et al. (2022) note 50–90% overlap of SPD with ASD, creating diagnostic conflation risk in both systems |
| **Differentiating power** | DSM-5's three-domain social communication requirement acts as a built-in filter against sensory-only diagnoses | ICD-11's integrated framework may reduce the discriminatory power against neurotypical individuals with strong sensory preferences or sensory-seeking behaviors that don't constitute clinical hypersensitivity | Kamp-Becker et al. (2024) critique ICD-11 for "hardly be differentiated from other mental disorders and autism-like traits" |

### Risk 2: Under-Diagnosis (Particularly in Females and Sensory-Predominant Presentations)

| Factor | Description | Evidence |
|---|---|---|

### Key Reimbursement Implications of ICD-11 Transition

1. **Loss of level-based benefit tier signaling**: DSM-5 severity levels (1/2/3) provided discrete insurance triggers. ICD-11 subtypes signal cognitive/language status but not directly support level. Payers must develop new mapping logic (e.g., case-by-case functional assessment overriding ICD code alone).

2. **Sensory-intervention coverage ambiguity**: Currently, OT reimbursement for sensory processing outside of ASD diagnosis is inconsistent across jurisdictions. Under ICD-11, if sensory dysregulation is a core ASD feature, sensory-focused OT sessions are more readily covered *when ASD is diagnosed*, but the boundary for non-AVD sensory work remains legally uncertain.

3. **Cross-border claims complexity**: Patients traveling across borders for treatment may encounter coding incompatibilities during transitions. Payer agreements will need explicit ICD-11 recognition clauses.

4. **Research funding and outcomes tracking**: Grant mechanisms and outcome databases tied to ICD-10 codes will require mapping updates. The shift from severity levels to subtype coding may affect how RCTs allocate participants and analyze endpoints.

## Evidence Gaps and Uncertainties

The following evidence gaps have been identified during this research compilation and represent areas where further investigation is needed:

1. **Direct head-to-head diagnostic accuracy comparison between DSM-5 and ICD-11 in live clinical settings**: No published study to date has measured DSM-5 and ICD-11 diagnostic sensitivity/specificity against a gold-standard assessment in the same population. The closest proxy (Wiggins et al., 2019) tested DSM-5 vs. DSM-IV-TR only. Future prospective validation studies involving clinicians applying both frameworks to identical patient presentations would substantially strengthen this evidence base.

2. **Quantified impact of ICD-11's undefined symptom threshold on inter-rater reliability**: Despite theoretical concerns (Kamp-Becker et al., 2024), no published study has empirically tested kappa statistics or interobserver agreement for ICD-11 ASD diagnoses compared to DSM-5 criteria in controlled settings.

3. **Gender-differentiated diagnostic accuracy by framework**: Existing research on female under-diagnosis (Gellert et al., 2025; Minutoli et al., 2025) examines biases in criteria derivation and clinical encounters but does not systematically compare detection rates using DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 criteria specifically. This gap disproportionately affects recommendations for improving equity.

4. **Longitudinal stability of ICD-11 subtypes vs. DSM-5 severity fluctuation**: It remains unknown whether ICD-11's static subtype assignment produces more brittle longitudinal tracking of clinical trajectories compared to DSM-5's flexible severity levels that can evolve over time.

5. **Integration of sensory processing assessment tools within ICD-11 diagnostic workflows**: While ICD-11 formally incorporates sensory disturbances, there are no validated ICD-11-aligned assessment instruments specifically for quantifying sensory phenotype severity within ASD diagnostic evaluations. Existing tools (e.g., SSRS sensory module, Sensory Profile) were not designed for ICD-11 integration.

6. **GRADE-quality assessment for diagnostic classification studies**: As noted, no formal GRADE rating system has been applied to comparative studies of DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 diagnostic frameworks. The field would benefit from consensus guidance on adapting GRADE methodology for nosological classification comparisons.

7. **U.S. payer-specific impact analysis post-ICD-11 adoption**: Given that U.S. ICD-11 clinical adoption is not yet finalized, there is no empirical data on how specific payers (Medicare, commercial insurers, Medicaid programs) will operationalize 6A02 codes for reimbursement, especially regarding the replacement of severity-level benefit triggers.

---

## Conclusion

The DSM-5 and ICD-11 represent philosophically aligned but structurally divergent approaches to diagnosing autism spectrum disorder. Both converge on the dual core of social communication deficits and restricted/repetitive behaviors and acknowledge late-emerging presentations with masking. However, their fundamental differences in **sensory processing weighting** (optional in DSM-5 vs. integrated into mandatory criteria in ICD-11), **symptom threshold precision** (explicit ≥2-of-4 rule vs. undefined count in ICD-11), **severity specification** (level-based support needs vs. cognitive-linguistic subtypes), and **model orientation** (behavioral-observable vs. experiential/social-model leaning) produce distinct risk profiles for diagnostic error and downstream clinical utilization.

For **sensory-predominant presentations**, the ICD-11 framework presents both opportunities (greater visibility for sensory-driven diagnoses) and risks (lower discriminative validity, potential over-attribution). The **APA and NICE** remain pragmatic, with NICE emphasizing equitable service access over manual specifics, while the **AAP** continues to reference DSM-5-TR criteria in U.S. clinical practice pending eventual ICD-11 transition. Advocacy organizations diverge sharply: neurodiversity-affirming groups (ASAN, National Autistic Society) prioritize person-centered understanding over taxonomic exactness, while the **medical-model advocate (Autism Speaks)** favors the DSM-5's functional impairment thresholds as a guardrail against diagnostic inflation.

Ultimately, the choice of framework influences not only who receives an ASD diagnosis but the type of support pathway, eligibility calculus, and therapeutic framing that follows. Clinicians navigating the current hybrid landscape (DSM-5-TR for U.S. clinical assessment; ICD-11 increasingly for global coding and EU administration) must recognize that the underlying philosophy of each system shapes interpretation beyond mere code lookup.

## Final Synthesis Statement

The DSM-5 (2013) and ICD-11 (2019) both seek to capture the heterogeneity of autism spectrum disorder, yet their structural divergence — most starkly in the **weighting of sensory processing** — has consequential implications for diagnostic gatekeeping, clinical equity, intervention appropriateness, and reimbursement logistics. The ICD-11's elevation of sensory disturbances from optional specifier to core mandatory feature broadens eligibility for sensory-predominant presentations, potentially improving identification for those whose social communication profile is milder but whose sensory dysregulation is functionally devastating. However, this structural shift comes at the cost of reduced diagnostic precision (undefined symptom thresholds, less falsifiable criteria), elevated false-positive risk, and challenges to established severity-based benefit structures in reimbursement systems.

Clinicians operating in the transitional zone between systems should remain attentive to: (1) the different operational thresholds each framework imposes on sensory-first presentations; (2) the risk that ICD-11's broader criteria will conflate autistic sensory profiles with non-autistic sensory-seeking behaviors; (3) the need for gender-sensitive assessment adaptations in both systems given persistent under-diagnosis of autistic girls and women; and (4) the reimbursement infrastructure lag behind the clinical classification evolution in the U.S., where ICD-10-CM F84 coding continues to govern benefits while ICD-11 6A02 advances internationally.

The most neurodiversity-affirming position — shared by ASAN and the National Autistic Society — is not strictly "ICD-11 over DSM-5" nor "DSM-5 over ICD-11," but rather the commitment to holistic, person-centered assessment that transcends manual taxonomy and centers lived experience, accessibility, and self-determination. Both manuals serve better as reference points than as definitive truth about autism; the responsible clinical stance involves using each framework's strengths while mitigating its known weaknesses, particularly the under-appreciation of sensory phenomenology in DSM-5-era assessments and the diagnostic vagueness inherent in ICD-11's current criterion structure.

# Comparative Analysis of Autism Diagnostic Criteria: DSM-5 (2013) vs. ICD-11 (2019)

---

## Executive Summary

This report provides a comprehensive comparison of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) diagnostic criteria between the American Psychiatric Association's DSM-5 (2013) and the World Health Organization's ICD-11 (2019), with particular attention to how each system defines and weights sensory processing differences. The two manuals share a foundational structure (core deficits in social communication plus restricted/repetitive patterns) but differ significantly in organizational philosophy, the mandatory versus optional status of sensory criteria, severity specification models, and downstream implications for clinical practice, advocacy, and reimbursement.

---

## Part A: Side-by-Side Criteria Comparison Table

| Criterion Element | DSM-5 (2013) | DSM-5-TR (2022 Revision) | ICD-11 (2019, effective Jan 2022) | Key Differences |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Core Domain 1: Social Communication Deficits** | **Criterion A**: "Persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts," manifested by deficits in (1) social-emotional reciprocity, (2) nonverbal communicative behaviors, (3) developing/maintaining relationships — **all three required** | Same wording; clarification changed "as manifested by" to **"as manifested by all of the following"** to require fulfillment of all three subdomains | **Feature 1**: "Persistent deficits in the ability to initiate and sustain reciprocal social interaction and social communication...outside the expected range" — includes deficits in understanding/integrating verbal and nonverbal cues, initiating conversations, responding socially, social awareness modulation, and making/sustaining peer relationships | Functionally equivalent core requirement; DSM-5 specifies three discrete domains, ICD-11 describes them more integratively but retains all components as essential |
| **Sensory Processing Definition & Weighting** | **Criterion B4** (one of four required under Criterion B): "Hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interests in sensory aspects of the environment" — examples include indifference to pain/temperature, adverse response to specific sounds/textures, excessive smelling/touching, visual fascination with lights/movement. **NOT required for diagnosis**; must meet ≥2 of four B-domain criteria, which may be any combination including only social communication deficits | Same as DSM-5-TR | Embedded within **Feature 2** (Restricted, repetitive patterns): "Lifelong excessive and persistent hypersensitivity or hyposensitivity to sensory stimuli or unusual interest in a sensory stimulus, including actual or anticipated sounds, light, textures (clothing/food), odours, tastes, heat, cold, or pain" — listed as **one manifestation of the mandatory restricted/repetitive pattern feature**, alongside routines, stereotypies, and special interests | **Critical distinction**: In DSM-5, sensory issues are an *optional* criterion (1 of 4); in ICD-11, sensory disturbances are formally part of the *required* diagnostic feature set. Someone with marked sensory dysregulation but few other restricted/repetitive behaviors would not qualify under DSM-5 (unless two other B-domains are met), but could qualify under ICD-11 if the sensory component meets the severity/threshold implied by "excessive and persistent" within the broader pattern requirement |
| **Restricted/Repetitive Behavior Requirement** | Must meet **≥2 of 4** criteria: (1) stereotyped movements/object use/speech, (2) insistence on sameness/routines, (3) restricted fixated interests, (4) sensory reactivity/unusual sensory interest | Same as DSM-5 | Must demonstrate persistent restricted/repetitive patterns "clearly atypical or excessive" — **number of specific manifestations not explicitly specified** in criteria; ~7 illustrative items listed (adaptability difficulty, routine rigidity, rule adherence, motor stereotypies, special interests, sensory hypersensitivity/hyposensitivity). **No minimum count mandated** | ICD-11 is more inclusive structurally; lacks a specified symptom threshold, generating clinical judgment variability. DSM-5's explicit "≥2 of 4" rule offers greater operational consistency |
| **Severity Specification** | Three severity levels based on current support needs: **Level 1** ("requiring support"): diminished social initiative; **Level 2** ("requiring substantial support"): difficulty with social interactions, obvious impairments; **Level 3** ("requires very substantial support"): severe verbal/nonverbal impairment, limited response to social approach | Same; minor clarification added | **No severity levels**. Instead, ICD-11 uses subtype specifications based on intellectual development and language capacity: 6A02.0 (without ID, mild/no language impairment), 6A02.1 (without ID, language impairment), 6A02.2 (with ID without impaired language functioning), 6A02.3 (with ID and impaired language), 6A02.4 (with ID and severely impaired language), 6A02.5 (with ID and absent functional language) | DSM-5 severity levels reflect *support needs*; ICD-11 subtypes reflect *cognitive/linguistic profile*. Different dimensional logic: DSM-5 severity can increase/decrease across lifespan; ICD-11 subtype is largely static upon diagnosis, though severity may still manifest within a subtype |
| **Age/Onset Requirements** | **Criterion C**: Symptoms must be present in the early developmental period (may not become fully manifest until social demands exceed capacities; may be masked in later life) | Same wording as DSM-5; slight refinement in DSM-5-TR clarity | **Feature 3**: "Onset of the disorder occurs during the developmental period – typically in early childhood – but characteristic symptoms may not become fully manifest until later when social demands exceed limited capacities" | Essentially identical in substance. Both acknowledge late emergence and masking. No requirement for age <3 years (unlike DSM-IV) |
| **Functional Impairment Threshold** | **Criterion D**: Symptoms cause "clinically significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of current functioning" | Same | **Feature 4**: Symptoms result in "significant impairment in personal, family, social, educational, occupational or other important areas of functioning." Acknowledges that exceptional effort may mask apparent deficits — diagnosis still appropriate despite adequate functioning through effort | Both require documented impairment. ICD-11 explicitly accommodates the "masking through exceptional effort" scenario (e.g., highly competent adults with undetectable symptoms), which DSM-5 allows implicitly via the "current functioning" phrasing but does not explicitly name masking |
| **Exclusion Criteria** | **Criterion E**: Not better explained by intellectual disability (ID) or global developmental delay. Comorbidity with ID is permitted if social communication deficits are below expected developmental level | Same | Not explicitly stated as a separate exclusion criterion but implicit in the overall framework; comorbidity with intellectual developmental disorder recognized and codified separately | Structure differs; DSM-5 lists as explicit criterion E, ICD-11 integrates this conceptually through its subtype structure |
| **Subtype Flexibility** | Unified single diagnosis ("autism spectrum disorder"); eliminates Asperger's as separate entity; "Specify if: with/without accompanying intellectual impairment" or "with/without accompanying language impairment" | Same; additional option added for "associated with another neurodevelopmental, mental, or behavioral disorder" | Five explicit subtypes based on ID and language status; unified diagnosis retained but with structured cognitive-linguistic stratification | ICD-11 provides more granular subtyping but less flexibility for specifying comorbidities beyond ID/language |

### Sensory Processing Deep-Dive Comparison

| Aspect | DSM-5 Position | ICD-11 Position | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Diagnostic necessity** | Optional (B4 = 1 of 4 required criteria); a person can meet ASD criteria without any sensory criterion | Included as a core manifestation within the mandatory restricted/repetitive behavior domain; implies stronger association between sensory phenotype and ASD diagnosis | ICD-11 signals that sensory dysfunction is considered part of the essential diagnostic syndrome, potentially lowering the threshold for sensory-driven presentations to qualify |
| **Scope definition** | Broad: hyper- or hyporeactivity; unusual *interests* in sensory aspects | Narrower operationalization: "excessive and persistent hypersensitivity or hyposensitivity"; "unusual interest in a sensory stimulus" — explicitly lists physical modalities (sounds, light, textures, odors, tastes, heat, cold, pain) | ICD-11 enumerates specific sensory modalities, potentially aiding clinical observation but reducing scope compared to DSM-5's open-ended formulation |
| **Temporal framing** | No explicit temporal modifier (though examples suggest chronic patterns) | States "lifelong" hypersensitivity or interest | ICD-11 reinforces developmental origin and chronicity, aligning with the early-onset principle but adding specificity |
| **Clinical utility for sensory-first presentations** | Lower — individuals presenting primarily with sensory challenges (minimal social communication deficits) face high risk of non-diagnosis unless other B-criteria are met | Higher — sensory dysregulation strengthens the case for ASD diagnosis within the existing restrictive-behavior framework even if fewer other criteria are evident | This represents a structural widening of eligibility for sensory-predominant profiles under ICD-11 |

---

## Part B: Evidence Synthesis — Peer-Reviewed Studies Comparing DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 Diagnostic Accuracy, Sensitivity/Specificity, or Clinical Utility

> **Note on GRADE Assessment**: GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations) quality ratings are formally designed for clinical interventions and diagnostic tests. Direct GRADE assessments of classification-system comparison studies are rare. Where cited, ratings reflect methodological limitations analogous to GRADE judgments for diagnostic accuracy studies. Authors of comparative analyses typically do not apply GRADE methodology per se. I provide estimated quality judgments based on study design, reporting transparency, and sample characteristics.

### Source 1: Wiggins, Lord, & Klin (2019) — Empirical Study of DSM-5 Sensitivity/Specificity

| Attribute | Detail |

| **Title** | "DSM-5 Criteria for Autism Spectrum Disorder Maximizes Diagnostic Sensitivity and Specificity in Preschool Children" |

## Part C: Clinical Guideline Positions on ICD-11 Adoption and Sensory Processing Weighting

### World Health Organization (WHO)

| Aspect | Position |
|---|---|
| **Classification stance** | WHO officially adopted ICD-11 effective 1 January 2022. ICD-11 6A02 (Autism Spectrum Disorder) became the global standard for morbidity coding. WHO has not issued a formal clinical guideline *advocating* ICD-11 over DSM-5 for autism diagnosis specifically; the decision rests with individual member states |
| **Implementation status** | As of mid-2025, WHO reported 50+ countries had entered different stages of ICD-11 implementation; full migration timelines vary. Many jurisdictions retain ICD-10 for administrative/billing while using ICD-11 for clinical coding |
| **Sensory processing framing** | WHO's ICD-11 clinical description explicitly includes sensory hypersensitivity/hyposensitivity as part of the required restricted/repetitive pattern. The WHO's 2024 CDDR (*Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Requirements for ICD-11 Mental, Behavioural and Neurodevelopmental Disorders*) codifies this inclusion. WHO guidance emphasizes phenotypic observation over dimensional severity scoring |
| **Guidance on assessment** | WHO fact sheet recommends comprehensive developmental assessment using standardized instruments, culturally adapted tools, and clinical judgment. No specific recommendation contrasting DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 assessment approaches is documented |

### American Psychiatric Association (APA)

| Aspect | Position |
|---|---|
| **Official standard** | APA maintains DSM-5-TR as its authoritative diagnostic reference (released 2022 revision). DSM-5-TR clarifies that all three social communication domains must be present and that the phrase "as manifested by" was changed to "as manifested by all of the following" to reinforce this requirement |
| **Stance on ICD-11** | APA does not formally oppose ICD-11 use. DSM-5-TR includes cross-reference to ICD-11 codes where applicable. APA acknowledges that ICD-11 and DSM-5 describe overlapping constructs but maintain DSM-5-TR as the professional standard for American psychiatric practice |
| **Sensory processing** | APA's diagnostic content does not elevate sensory processing beyond Criterion B4's optional status. APA has not addressed the structural difference between DSM-5's optional sensory criterion and ICD-11's mandatory inclusion. The APA's *Practice Guidelines for the Assessment and Treatment of Individuals With Autism Spectrum Disorders* (2019 update) notes sensory difficulties as common comorbid features requiring evaluation but does not tie them directly to diagnostic thresholds |
| **Neurodiversity acknowledgment** | APA has historically maintained a biomedical/frameworthy stance but has acknowledged increasing influence of neurodiversity perspectives in recent publications and positions |

### American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP)

| Aspect | Position |
|---|---|
| **Primary guidance** | AAP clinical report (*Identification, Evaluation, and Management of Children With Autism Spectrum Disorders*, 2020 update, reaffirmed 2026): Recommends developmental screening at 14, 18, and 24 months using M-CHAT-R/F; immediate referral to intervention for any positive screen or parental concern; diagnostic evaluation guided by current criteria (primarily DSM-5-TR in U.S. context) |
| **Coding stance** | AAP guidance references clinical diagnosis criteria without prescribing a specific classification system. In practice, U.S. pediatricians code using ICD-10-CM (currently F84.x) for billing purposes |
| **Sensory processing** | AAP recognizes that sensory processing difficulties frequently co-occur with ASD and contribute to behavior challenges. The 2020 report mentions evaluating sensory regulation as part of comprehensive assessment but does not specify how ICD-11's elevated sensory weighting should alter pediatric assessment protocols |
| **ICD-11 consideration** | AAP has not issued formal guidance addressing the transition to ICD-11 coding for autism in U.S. primary care settings. Given projected U.S. adoption timeline (likely 2025–2027 for clinical/mortality coding), no actionable guidance currently exists |

### National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE, UK)

| Aspect | Position |
|---|---|
| **Guidelines** | NICE Clinical Guideline CG128 (2011, periodic review pending) covers recognition and diagnosis of ASD in under-19s; CG142 (2012, updated) covers adults. Both emphasize: early identification through developmental screening; multidisciplinary team assessment using validated instruments (ADOS-2, ADI-R, etc.); referral triggers based on screening concerns, not specific coding system |
| **Diagnostic system stance** | NICE states diagnostic criteria should follow either DSM-5 or ICD-11 frameworks; the guideline does not prescribe one over the other and focuses on competency of assessors rather than the classification system employed. UK NHS digital health records systems are transitioning to accommodate ICD-11 codes progressively |
| **Sensory processing** | NICE CG128/CG142 explicitly recommends investigating sensory issues as contributors to challenging behaviors and recommending environmental adjustments (lighting, noise reduction, sensory strategies) as part of management plans. NICE has endorsed sensory processing considerations within an autism support context regardless of diagnostic code |
| **Neurodiversity alignment** | NICE materials consistently frame autism within a neurodiversity lens, describing autistic people as "neurodiverse" and emphasizing rights, access, and dignity over deficit modeling |

## Part E: Diagnostic Safety Risks — Misdiagnosis, Over-, Under-Diagnosis, and Inappropriate Interventions

### Overview of Risk Landscape

The structural differences between DSM-5 and ICD-11 create divergent risk profiles for diagnostic errors, particularly for presentations dominated by sensory processing difficulties with comparatively attenuated social communication deficits.

### Risk 1: Over-Diagnosis and False Positive Rates

| Factor | DSM-5 Risk Profile | ICD-11 Risk Profile | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Symptom threshold** | Requires ≥2 of 4 B-domain symptoms; sensory criterion optional — thus a sensory-predominant presentation with only one other behavioral marker (e.g., mild routine preference) fails criteria | No explicit minimum symptom count; sensory hypersensitivity embedded within mandatory restricted-repetitive domain lowers practical threshold for sensory-driven presentations | Kamp-Becker et al. (2024) predict elevated false-positive risk under ICD-11's undefined-count approach; Greaves-Lord et al. (2022) note consultative debate about appropriate threshold |
| **Historical prevalence trends** | DSM-5-era diagnosis rates increased approximately 2-fold from 2013–2018 (Kulage et al., 2020, meta-analysis of 33 studies) | If ICD-11's lower threshold takes hold, further upward pressure on prevalence is plausible, though real prevalence vs. detection-rate separation remains contested | Kulage et al. (2020), PubMed PMID 30852784 |
| **Sensory-specific over-identification** | Individuals with pronounced sensory sensitivities but ambiguous social communication profiles face high risk of receiving ASD diagnosis via sensory pathway only under DSM-5 if a second B-domain coincidentally emerges; otherwise may receive SPD treatment (standalone) or no diagnosis | ICD-11 may lead to broader ASD attribution for individuals previously classified under non-specific sensory/behavioral categories, with less differentiation from ADHD, selective mutism, or anxiety-driven sensory avoidance | Passarello et al. (2022) note 50–90% overlap of SPD with ASD, creating diagnostic conflation risk in both systems |
| **Differentiating power** | DSM-5's three-domain social communication requirement acts as a built-in filter against sensory-only diagnoses | ICD-11's integrated framework may reduce the discriminatory power against neurotypical individuals with strong sensory preferences or sensory-seeking behaviors that don't constitute clinical hypersensitivity | Kamp-Becker et al. (2024) critique ICD-11 for "hardly be differentiated from other mental disorders and autism-like traits" |

### Risk 2: Under-Diagnosis (Particularly in Females and Sensory-Predominant Presentations)

| Factor | Description | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **Female under-diagnosis** | Girls often mask social communication deficits throughcamouflaging, presenting with subtler external signs. DSM-5 criteria developed from predominantly male samples. ICD-11 retains similar criteria structure; neither system explicitly adjusts for gender-related masking effects | Gellert et al. (2025), "Underdiagnosed and Misunderstood: Clinical Challenges and Gender Disparities" (PMC12382651); Minutoli et al. (2025), Frontiers in Psychiatry systematic analysis of female underdiagnosis |
| **Sensory-first presentations in females** | Girls may exhibit sensory processing difficulties (hyperreactivity to sounds, textures, lights) as primary presenting feature with minimal initial social complaint, leading to delayed ASD identification | Multiple observational studies document sensory problems as frequent primary complaints in mothers seeking evaluation for picky eating, sleep disruption, or anxiety in girls; linkage to ASD confirmation is inconsistent |
| **Adult late-diagnosis delays** | Adult autistic individuals—particularly women, Black individuals, and those with average or above-average intelligence—face prolonged under-identification. The DSM-5's early-onset requirement, while relaxed, still poses barriers. ICD-11 similarly requires onset "during the developmental period" without explicit allowance for extreme late emergence | Marques et al. (2025) systematic review on late ASD diagnosis in women; general literature on adult autismo diagnosis delays |

### Risk 3: Misdiagnosis Conflation

| Misdiagnosis Pattern | Mechanism | Interaction with Criteria Systems |
|---|---|---|
| **ASD ↔ ADHD confusion** | Shared features: distractibility, sensory aversions, task persistence, social frustration | Both systems recognize these features but define distinct core domains. ICD-11's reduced strictness may increase misclassification risk; DSM-5's stricter social communication requirement theoretically improves separation but does not eliminate overlap (comorbidity is high and bidirectional) |
| **Sensory Regulation Disorder → ASD vs. Reverse** | SPD is not recognized in either DSM-5 or ICD-11 as a standalone diagnosis; symptoms frequently attributed to either ASD or to "poor sensory processing" outside diagnostic frameworks | Passarello et al. (2022) highlight diagnostic uncertainty in this zone; the optional-but-present nature of DSM-5 B4 creates ambiguity, while ICD-11's mandatory inclusion shifts direction |
| **Anxiety-driven sensory avoidance → ASD** | Children with anxiety who avoid sensory inputs (to reduce fear rather than hypersensitivity) may be assessed for ASD; reverse scenario also occurs: ASD children develop anxiety secondary to sensory overload | Neither system captures the motivational qualifier ("aversive versus hypersensitive"), risking misinterpretation of sensory behavior drivers |
| **High-functioning individuals without impairment → ASD** | Highly capable adults with mild social preferences and organized sensory interests may meet ICD-11's lowered threshold for "persistent restricted/repetitive patterns" if sensory involvement is prominent | DSM-5's explicit functional impairment requirement (Criterion D) serves as a safeguard; ICD-11 acknowledges masking through effort but does not add an impairment-weighted threshold comparable to DSM-5 Level requirements |

### Risk 4: Inappropriate or Misaligned Interventions

| Intervention Risk | DSM-5 Context | ICD-11 Context | Evidence/Guidance |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sensory Integration Therapy (SIT)** | Widely offered for sensory issues associated with ASD, but evidence base limited; SIT not recommended as evidence-based treatment by USPSTF/NICE for ASD-associated sensory problems. May be provided regardless of whether sensory criterion was a factor in diagnosis | Increased likelihood of SIT referral driven by ICD-11's prominence of sensory dysregulation within the diagnostic core, even for presentations where sensory issues were secondary or not clinically significant for functional impairment | NICE does not recommend SIT as first-line; Cochrane reviews show mixed evidence (Camino-Alarcón et al., 2024 MDPI review notes growing but inconsistent evidence base) |
| **Medication for sensory discomfort** | Rarely targeted at sensory hypersensitivity pharmacologically; antipsychotics sometimes used for dysregulatory outbursts in severe cases | ICD-11's emphasis on sensory distress as core may spur greater attempts at medication targeting sensory modulation, an area with limited evidence and significant safety considerations (especially children) | No authoritative body supports routine pharmacotherapy for sensory processing differences; FDA-approved medications for sensory symptoms do not exist |
| **Educational accommodations triggered by diagnosis** | DSM-5 diagnosis unlocks IEP/504 rights under U.S. law; eligibility depends on demonstrating impact in educational functioning | ICD-11 diagnosis carries equivalent legal/access implications once adopted by payers; however, broader diagnostic catchment may create uneven application of accommodations across jurisdiction lines | Legal frameworks (IDEA in US, Equality Act/Disability Discrimination Act in UK) determine accommodation rights independently of coding system |
| **Therapy modality mismatches** | Standard ABA, speech therapy, occupational therapy may or may not incorporate sensory-focused components depending on clinician training | ICD-11 framing may encourage OTs to prioritize sensory regulation approaches, potentially diverting focus from evidence-based communication-focused interventions | Mixed evidence base for sensory-focused interventions; strongest evidence for communication-focused interventions (Lord et al., NEJM 2020) |

### Summary Risk Matrix

| Risk Category | Elevated under DSM-5 | Elevated under ICD-11 | Direction of Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Over-diagnosis / false positives | Moderate (due to lowered age requirement and subtype unification) | **High** (undefined symptom threshold; sensory inclusion broadens eligibility) | ↑↑ Increase |
| Under-diagnosis in females | Moderate (masking bias in criteria derivation) | Moderate (similar risk; ICD-11 does not address gender differential explicitly) | Stable |
| Sensory-first misclassification | Moderate (sensory optional; requires concurrence with other markers) | **High** (sensory central; may suffice within pattern framework) | ↑↑ Increase |
| Diagnostic uncertainty in borderline cases | Moderate | **High** (subjective weighting without quantified thresholds) | ↑↑ Increase |
| Inappropriate sensory-targeted interventions | Low-Moderate | Moderate (may inflate therapeutic intent for sensory work) | ↑ Slight increase |

Diagnosis code determines authorization prerequisites | Similar structure anticipated; however, if sensory issues gain weight within 6A02 coding, OT claims may face scrutiny regarding whether sensory work constitutes "standard ASD-managed" therapy vs. standalone SPD service (which is currently not coverable) |

### European Union (ECDC/EU Health Information Standards)

| Component | Current/ICD-10 Context | ICD-11 Adoption Trajectory |
|---|---|---|
| **Coding system** | Member states vary: some use ICD-10, others already adopting ICD-11. ECDC surveillance data primarily uses ICD-10-coded diagnoses for epidemiological tracking | Progressive national adoption. By 2025, majority of EU member states active in ICD-11 implementation for clinical and statistical purposes |
| **Primary code mapping** | ICD-10 F84.x codes mapped to ICD-11 6A02 family. Crosswalk tables provided by WHO facilitate conversion. ICD-10 subcategories (F84.0 autism, F84.5 Asperger's) collapse into unified 6A02 umbrella with subtype descriptors | Europe has embraced the unified ASD category aligned with ICD-11 structure. National health registries (e.g., Sweden's SIR, UK's DHSC data) updating to 6A02 codes |

Functional coverage models (based on need for support/intervention type) predominate over code-specific financial entitlements. Sensory-related interventions (OT, speech) remain coverable as part of ASD management packages |
| **Statistical comparability** | Cross-national prevalence analyses complicated by inconsistent ICD versions in reporting periods | ICD-11 harmonization intended to improve international comparability; however, ongoing debate about whether 6A02's broader thresholds will alter reported prevalence upward |
| **National Autism Registries** | Several countries (Sweden, Netherlands, UK) maintain autism registers; register definitions often reference specific ICD codes but prioritize phenotypic description over code taxonomy | Registers transitioning to ICD-11 coding for new entries; historical data backmapped where possible |

### Key Reimbursement Implications of ICD-11 Transition

1. **Loss of level-based benefit tier signaling**: DSM-5 severity levels (1/2/3) provided discrete insurance triggers. ICD-11 subtypes signal cognitive/language status but not directly support level. Payers must develop new mapping logic (e.g., case-by-case functional assessment overriding ICD code alone).

2. **Sensory-intervention coverage ambiguity**: Currently, OT reimbursement for sensory processing outside of ASD diagnosis is inconsistent across jurisdictions. Under ICD-11, if sensory dysregulation is a core ASD feature, sensory-focused OT sessions are more readily covered *when ASD is diagnosed*, but the boundary for non-AVD sensory work remains legally uncertain.

3. **Cross-border claims complexity**: Patients traveling across borders for treatment may encounter coding incompatibilities during transitions. Payer agreements will need explicit ICD-11 recognition clauses.

4. **Research funding and outcomes tracking**: Grant mechanisms and outcome databases tied to ICD-10 codes will require mapping updates. The shift from severity levels to subtype coding may affect how RCTs allocate participants and analyze endpoints.

## Evidence Gaps and Uncertainties

The following evidence gaps have been identified during this research compilation and represent areas where further investigation is needed:

1. **Direct head-to-head diagnostic accuracy comparison between DSM-5 and ICD-11 in live clinical settings**: No published study to date has measured DSM-5 and ICD-11 diagnostic sensitivity/specificity against a gold-standard assessment in the same population. The closest proxy (Wiggins et al., 2019) tested DSM-5 vs. DSM-IV-TR only. Future prospective validation studies involving clinicians applying both frameworks to identical patient presentations would substantially strengthen this evidence base.

2. **Quantified impact of ICD-11's undefined symptom threshold on inter-rater reliability**: Despite theoretical concerns (Kamp-Becker et al., 2024), no published study has empirically tested kappa statistics or interobserver agreement for ICD-11 ASD diagnoses compared to DSM-5 criteria in controlled settings.

3. **Gender-differentiated diagnostic accuracy by framework**: Existing research on female under-diagnosis (Gellert et al., 2025; Minutoli et al., 2025) examines biases in criteria derivation and clinical encounters but does not systematically compare detection rates using DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 criteria specifically. This gap disproportionately affects recommendations for improving equity.

4. **Longitudinal stability of ICD-11 subtypes vs. DSM-5 severity fluctuation**: It remains unknown whether ICD-11's static subtype assignment produces more brittle longitudinal tracking of clinical trajectories compared to DSM-5's flexible severity levels that can evolve over time.

5. **Integration of sensory processing assessment tools within ICD-11 diagnostic workflows**: While ICD-11 formally incorporates sensory disturbances, there are no validated ICD-11-aligned assessment instruments specifically for quantifying sensory phenotype severity within ASD diagnostic evaluations. Existing tools (e.g., SSRS sensory module, Sensory Profile) were not designed for ICD-11 integration.

6. **GRADE-quality assessment for diagnostic classification studies**: As noted, no formal GRADE rating system has been applied to comparative studies of DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 diagnostic frameworks. The field would benefit from consensus guidance on adapting GRADE methodology for nosological classification comparisons.

7. **U.S. payer-specific impact analysis post-ICD-11 adoption**: Given that U.S. ICD-11 clinical adoption is not yet finalized, there is no empirical data on how specific payers (Medicare, commercial insurers, Medicaid programs) will operationalize 6A02 codes for reimbursement, especially regarding the replacement of severity-level benefit triggers.

---

## Conclusion

The DSM-5 and ICD-11 represent philosophically aligned but structurally divergent approaches to diagnosing autism spectrum disorder. Both converge on the dual core of social communication deficits and restricted/repetitive behaviors and acknowledge late-emerging presentations with masking. However, their fundamental differences in **sensory processing weighting** (optional in DSM-5 vs. integrated into mandatory criteria in ICD-11), **symptom threshold precision** (explicit ≥2-of-4 rule vs. undefined count in ICD-11), **severity specification** (level-based support needs vs. cognitive-linguistic subtypes), and **model orientation** (behavioral-observable vs. experiential/social-model leaning) produce distinct risk profiles for diagnostic error and downstream clinical utilization.

For **sensory-predominant presentations**, the ICD-11 framework presents both opportunities (greater visibility for sensory-driven diagnoses) and risks (lower discriminative validity, potential over-attribution). The **APA and NICE** remain pragmatic, with NICE emphasizing equitable service access over manual specifics, while the **AAP** continues to reference DSM-5-TR criteria in U.S. clinical practice pending eventual ICD-11 transition. Advocacy organizations diverge sharply: neurodiversity-affirming groups (ASAN, National Autistic Society) prioritize person-centered understanding over taxonomic exactness, while the **medical-model advocate (Autism Speaks)** favors the DSM-5's functional impairment thresholds as a guardrail against diagnostic inflation.

Ultimately, the choice of framework influences not only who receives an ASD diagnosis but the type of support pathway, eligibility calculus, and therapeutic framing that follows. Clinicians navigating the current hybrid landscape (DSM-5-TR for U.S. clinical assessment; ICD-11 increasingly for global coding and EU administration) must recognize that the underlying philosophy of each system shapes interpretation beyond mere code lookup.
